property_summary: Before initialization, SetMinSum persists the argument in the public MinSum variable; after initialization the call must fail.

After a successful Collect, MinSum remains unchanged in the buggy version (so previous calls to SetMinSum are ineffective), whereas in the reference version MinSum reflects the value set via SetMinSum.
After any sequence of SetMinSum and Collect, the stored MinSum must equal the last value passed to SetMinSum; the bug makes it always zero because the assignment targets a local variable.

In the reference contract, MinSum is settable before initialization via SetMinSum and its value persists after initialization; in the buggy version, SetMinSum writes to a local variable, so MinSum never changes from its initial value of 0 no matter how many times SetMinSum is called.

After a non-reverting Collect call under the minimum balance condition, the contract's MinSum must equal the last value passed to SetMinSum (before initialization); the buggy version leaves MinSum at zero because the assignment targets a local variable.
After initialization and a successful Collect, MinSum equals the value set via SetMinSum before initialization; the bug makes MinSum remain 0 because the assignment targets a local variable.
If SetMinSum is called with a nonzero value before initialization, then after initialization MinSum is nonzero.
After two calls to SetMinSum with different values, where the first call would have reverted on P due to nonReentrant modifier, the second call's input becomes the stored MinSum.
Collect can be reentered via its external call to withdraw funds, potentially altering MinSum mid-execution in the mutant but not in the original.

A state-changing call on C that succeeds must execute without any prior state-changing call in the same transaction having bypassed a revert, so any revert-free successful call implies the contract was not reentered through a removed modifier check.
In a single transaction, MinSum cannot be changed after a successful Collect call, because the original prevents reentrant state changes.
After a successful Collect call that sends ether, MinSum must remain unchanged because the nonReentrant modifier prevents reentrant state modifications during the external call.
The MinSum stored in C can never change after initialization is complete, but the mutant allows a reentrant call to SetMinSum through Collect's external call, altering MinSum.

After initialization, MinSum must remain strictly immutable across any sequence of calls to Collect, but the mutant allows a reentrant actor to reset MinSum via a Collect-triggered fallback, breaking immutability.
After initialization is complete, MinSum must remain unchanged across any Collect call, but the mutant allows a reentrant caller to reset MinSum during the external call in Collect.
After initialization is complete, the value of MinSum must remain unchanged; the bug allows a reentrant attacker to call SetMinSum via Collect's external call, changing MinSum.

After initialization, the state variable MinSum must reflect the last call to SetMinSum; the buggy SetMinSum never updates MinSum, so reading MinSum after a call to SetMinSum with a non-zero argument yields the previous value instead of the argument.

After the contract is initialized and SetMinSum is called with a non-zero value, MinSum must equal that value; the buggy version ignores the argument, so MinSum remains unchanged from the previous value.

After initialization and a non-reverting call to SetMinSum with a value v (while the contract is not locked), the public getter MinSum() must equal v; the buggy version never updates the state variable, so MinSum remains 0 (its default), violating the property for v > 0.

After the contract is initialized and SetMinSum is called with a value v, MinSum must equal v; the buggy version ignores the parameter, so MinSum stays at its previous value, violating the rule for any v different from the previous MinSum.

For EVERY possible sequence of calls, the SetLogFile function can only be invoked when the contract is not locked due to reentrancy protection; removing the nonReentrant_ modifier allows it to be called during an active lock, violating this invariant.

For any admissible call sequence, if intitalized is true then SetLogFile should always revert (whether locked or not); removing the reentrancy guard allows SetLogFile to succeed during an active reentrancy lock when intitalized is false, breaking the invariant that the guard prevents execution while locked.

After the contract is initialized, any call to SetLogFile must revert (because the nonReentrant_ modifier would enforce locked_==false, but intitalized==true causes revert). Removing the modifier allows SetLogFile to be called during an active lock when intitalized is false, then later when initialized is true it should always revert, but the bug makes it succeed during reentrancy.

Throughout the entire lifecycle of the contract, if a call to SetLogFile succeeds without reverting, the reentrancy lock must be false immediately after the call returns; the bug allows SetLogFile to succeed while the lock is true during a reentrant call, violating this invariant.

Whenever SetLogFile is called, if the call does not revert, the reentrancy lock (locked_) must be false afterward; the bug allows SetLogFile to succeed during an active reentrant call, so locked_ may remain true.

For any call to SetLogFile, exactly one entry is added to the Log's History array; the buggy version lacking the require(!locked_) check allows a reentrant callback to add more than one entry per external call.
